WorldDraft: If Code Builds the World, Can Video Models Just Render It?

Zhiyu Hou    Wen-Jie Shu    Harold H. Chen    Weilin Ruan    Chenfei Liao    Liuzhou Zhang    Disen Lan    Xiaogang Xu    Qi Chen    Ser-Nam Lim Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [
Abstract

Multimodal coding agents decouple 4D world construction from visual generation, repurposing video models from world generators toward generative renderers. This division of labor raises a fundamental question: if code builds the world, can video models just render it? A reliable generative renderer hinges on two complementary criteria: (i) world preservation, retaining prescribed 4D kinematics and camera paths; and (ii) visual realization, persistently binding text-specified target attributes over time. To evaluate this capability, we introduce WorldDraft, a benchmark of 432432 strictly paired test cases across 4848 executable 4D world families spanning six dynamic challenge categories. Under a 3×33\times 3 factorial design, WorldDraft orthogonally crosses draft granularity (abstract proxy to previs) and appearance alignment (neutral to conflicting) under identical dynamics. Extensive evaluations across 1212 representative models reveal that: (I) world preservation and visual realization remain in stark operational tension; (II) richer draft scaffolding anchors structure but paradoxically impairs appearance fidelity; and (III) conflicting source cues trigger severe source leakage (up to 64%64\%), exposing fragile cross-modal disentanglement. To mitigate these bottlenecks, we propose WorldDraft-Primer, a plug-and-play visual prompting strategy that consistently improves both objectives across frozen video renderers. Together, WorldDraft and WorldDraft-Primer lay a foundation for bridging programmatic 4D simulation with video generation, advancing physically grounded generative rendering.

1 Introduction

Video generation has achieved remarkable progress in visual realism and temporal coherence, yet generating complex, controllable dynamic scenes remains challenging (Wan et al., 2025; Agarwal et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026a; HaCohen et al., 2024). Since end-to-end models must implicitly infer 4D world evolution from brief text while simultaneously generating pixels, high visual quality often comes at the expense of physical and spatiotemporal reliability. Recently, advances in multimodal coding agents have enabled an alternative paradigm that decouples world construction from visual generation (Li et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026a; Liang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026). By programmatically controlling engines such as Blender (Blender Online Community, 2026) or MuJoCo (Todorov et al., 2012), coding agents can explicitly specify scene layouts, object trajectories, and physical interactions as executable simulation drafts, leaving video generation models to transform these low-fidelity drafts into photorealistic videos.

This emerging division of labor explores repurposing video models from world generators toward generative renderers, raising a fundamental question: if code builds the world, can video models just render it? We thus argue that a reliable generative renderer hinges on fulfilling two complementary objectives: ❶ world preservation, which demands faithfully retaining the scene geometry, object dynamics, event timing, and camera motion prescribed by the draft without rewriting the underlying world; and ❷ visual realization, which requires accurately generating text-specified target attributes (e.g., color, material) while persistently binding them to the corresponding 4D entities across motion, occlusion, and viewpoint changes.

Formally, generative rendering operates as a conditional video-to-video (V2V) transformation guided by a structural draft and a target text prompt, yet existing benchmarks only partially address its requirements. Early V2V benchmarks (Li et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026) focus on editing real-world videos that already possess rich source textures, whereas recent programmable-world evaluation (Huang et al., 2026) primarily examines whether generated videos follow program-logged states and interaction events. Crucially, achieving world preservation does not guarantee faithful visual realization: models frequently retain coarse draft dynamics while failing to generate or temporally bind target appearance, or conversely fulfill appearance prompts at the cost of altering the underlying 4D world. This gap motivates the need for a new benchmark that jointly evaluates both objectives to systematically characterize the capability boundaries of generative renderers.

In this work, we propose WorldDraft, a systematic benchmark designed to evaluate video models as draft-to-video generative renderers through three progressive questions (Figure 2). First, ➀ can video models render target appearances without corrupting complex 4D worlds? To test this foundational capability, we curate 4848 executable 4D world families spanning ♣ six challenge categories: multi-entity orchestration, multi-stage dynamics, occlusion and reappearance, camera motion, non-rigid deformation, and hybrid interactions. Grounded in explicit simulator references, WorldDraft jointly measures how faithfully a model preserves the prescribed 4D structure and how accurately it realizes and persistently binds target visual attributes over time. Building upon these base worlds, we further probe the capability boundaries of generative renderers along two complementary axes: ➁ how much information must a draft provide to support reliable rendering? We then instantiate each world across ♠ three draft granularity levels (ranging from abstract proxies to detailed previews) to quantify minimal input requirements and the gains from richer structural and visual cues; and ➂ can models disentangle the world structure to preserve from the source appearance to overwrite? We further pair each draft with ♠ three appearance alignment levels (neutral, aligned, and conflicting) under a shared target prompt to evaluate selective adherence to structural versus textual conditions. Crossing both axes across all 4848 world families yields a unified 3×33\times 3 factorial design of 432432 strictly paired test cases.

Through extensive evaluation on WorldDraft, we observe that existing video models struggle to jointly preserve underlying 4D worlds and realize persistent target appearances, especially under coarse draft granularity or conflicting source-target cues (see Figure 1). Motivated by these findings, we further propose WorldDraft-Primer, a plug-and-play visual prompting strategy designed to enhance frozen video renderers. Unlike existing adaptation pipelines that rely on costly retraining or privileged simulator access (Li et al., 2026b; Gomez-Nogales et al., 2026), WorldDraft-Primer operates solely on the input draft and target prompt. Specifically, it injects subtle visual cues into the first draft frame via two complementary strategies: (i) object emphasis, which highlights key or easily overlooked entities to reinforce world preservation; and (ii) attribute cueing, which encodes target colors, textures, and shading cues around entities and supporting surfaces to guide visual realization. Experiments show that WorldDraft-Primer consistently boosts performance across diverse models, serving as both an analytical companion to WorldDraft and a practical solution for improving draft-to-video generative rendering.

To summarize, this work contributes threefold:

  • •

    We propose WorldDraft, a systematic benchmark for draft-to-video generative rendering comprising 432432 strictly paired test cases across 4848 executable 4D world families, organized across six challenge categories and a 3×33\times 3 factorial grid of draft granularity and appearance alignment levels.

  • •

    Through extensive experiments across 1212 representative video models, our findings highlight that: (i) world preservation and visual realization remain in stark operational tension; (ii) finer draft granularity anchors structure but paradoxically impairs appearance fidelity; and (iii) conflicting source cues cause severe source leakage, exposing fragile source-target disentanglement.

  • •

    We further introduce WorldDraft-Primer, a simple yet effective plug-and-play visual prompting strategy that injects object emphasis and attribute cues into the first draft frame, consistently boosting both world preservation and visual realization across frozen video renderers.

2 Related Work

Code-for-Vision.

Emerging works explore executable code as an intermediate representation for 3D reconstruction and scene synthesis (Yin et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b; Huang et al., 2024a), driving graphics engines to explicitly control geometry, camera parameters, and lighting. Extending this paradigm to dynamic environments, frameworks such as GS-Agent (Zhang et al., 2026) and Code as Worlds (Wang et al., 2026a) describe 4D physical evolution in code, relying on simulators to govern deterministic trajectories and interaction rules. This approach establishes a modular division of labor: systems like VideoCoCo (Li et al., 2026b) and Code Video Model (Liang et al., 2026) also employ coding agents to construct simulation drafts, leaving video generation models to synthesize photorealistic outputs. While prior research primarily targets upstream world construction, WorldDraft focuses on the downstream rendering stage, evaluating whether video models can faithfully realize target appearances without corrupting the underlying executable world.

Evaluation of Video-to-Video.

V2V evaluation has traditionally focused on text-guided editing, measuring instruction adherence, temporal consistency, and background preservation on natural videos (Chen et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2026). With the rise of programmatic generation, recent benchmarks such as PROWBench (Huang et al., 2026) check behavioral fidelity and event timelines against engine-logged states while evaluating visual quality through holistic metrics such as CLIP. However, such holistic evaluations overlook whether models can faithfully realize fine-grained target attributes and persistently bind them across dynamic 4D processes. In this work, WorldDraft goes a step further by investigating how varying input conditions govern the interplay between world preservation and appearance realization.

3 WorldDraft

3.1 Task Formulation

Generative Rendering.

Programmatic video generation decouples physical reasoning from visual generation: upstream engines explicitly govern scene kinematics, leaving downstream video models to act as renderers. Formally, an upstream simulator executes an underlying 4D world 𝒲\mathcal{W} to yield a draft video 𝒟={𝐈tsrc}t=1T∈ℝT×H×W×3\mathcal{D}=\{\mathbf{I}_{t}^{\text{src}}\}_{t=1}^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times H\times W\times 3}. Given 𝒟\mathcal{D} and a target prompt 𝐩\mathbf{p}, a generative renderer 𝒢\mathcal{G} synthesizes the target video:

𝒱^=𝒢⁡(𝒟,𝐩),\hat{\mathcal{V}}=\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{D},\mathbf{p}), (1)

where 𝒟\mathcal{D} provides the 4D spatiotemporal scaffold (e.g., geometry, kinematics, camera), and 𝐩\mathbf{p} dictates target visual attributes (e.g., color, material, lighting). At inference, 𝒢\mathcal{G} strictly accesses (𝒟,𝐩)(\mathcal{D},\mathbf{p}), with 𝒲\mathcal{W} reserved solely for draft generation and ground-truth evaluation references.

Dual Criteria.

To determine whether 𝒢\mathcal{G} faithfully executes this conditional transformation, the correctness of generative rendering hinges on two criteria:

  1. ❏

    World Preservation, requiring 𝒱^\hat{\mathcal{V}} to faithfully preserve the prescribed 4D kinematics, entity identities, event timelines, and camera motion in 𝒟\mathcal{D} without prompt-countermanded structural hallucinations.

  2. ❏

    Visual Realization, requiring 𝒱^\hat{\mathcal{V}} to accurately instantiate target attributes from 𝐩\mathbf{p} and persistently bind them to corresponding entities across dynamic motion, occlusions, and viewpoint changes.

Generative rendering thus demands that 𝒢\mathcal{G} disentangle the world structure to preserve from the source appearance to overwrite: a capability fundamentally governed by the draft’s input condition.

3.2 Executable World Families

Challenge Taxonomy.

To evaluate renderers beyond trivial rigid motions, candidate worlds should enforce deterministic physical constraints for world preservation while imposing dynamic stressors for visual realization. Guided by these principles, we first establish 4848 executable world families across six primary categories (Figure 2):

These categories serve as primary stressors rather than disjoint splits; each family is classified by its dominant challenge while incorporating secondary dynamics. In particular, multi-entity orchestration focuses on cooperative spatial topology, whereas hybrid interactions stresses dynamic physical coupling between contact processes.

Construction and Validation.

For each challenge, we first collect diverse real-world videos as dynamic blueprints, and employ multimodal coding agents (i.e., GPT-6-Astra (Singh et al., 2025)) to translate their underlying physical interactions and camera paths into executable MuJoCo (Todorov et al., 2012) or Blender (Blender Online Community, 2026) scripts. Crucially, the footage serves as world reference rather than a target for pixel-level reconstruction. Execution produces deterministic 4D rollouts while programmatically logging the ground-truth state tuple:

𝒲i=(𝒮i,𝒯i,ℰi,𝒞i),\mathcal{W}_{i}=(\mathcal{S}_{i},\mathcal{T}_{i},\mathcal{E}_{i},\mathcal{C}_{i}), (2)

with 3D geometry 𝒮i\mathcal{S}_{i}, dense trajectories 𝒯i\mathcal{T}_{i}, event timestamps ℰi\mathcal{E}_{i}, and camera poses 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i}. Each world passes a three-tiered admission audit: ➀ numerical stability without divergence, ➁ fidelity to the reference interaction, and ➂ evaluative viability with unambiguous 4D binding stressors, freezing 4848 standardized families, as shown in Figure 3.

3.3 Controlled Draft Design

To further isolate whether rendering failures stem from insufficient structural support or deceptive appearance cues, we then freeze the 4D kinematics and prompt 𝐩i\mathbf{p}_{i} for each 𝒲i\mathcal{W}_{i}, and further orthogonally vary drafts across two axes: draft granularity and appearance alignment.

Prompt Suite.

A unified prompt 𝐩i\mathbf{p}_{i} per family specifies 2∼42\sim 4 verifiable attributes (e.g., color, material, lighting). To guarantee unbiased evaluation, 𝐩i\mathbf{p}_{i} enforces: ➀ observable verification via unambiguous visual criteria; ➁ alignment-invariant references that index entities via spatial/semantic roles (e.g., “leading cube”) rather than volatile appearance tags; and ➂ structural neutrality, strictly omitting trajectories or camera paths so text cannot compensate for draft sparsity. More examples are in Appendix A.

Draft Granularity (PP).

To investigate minimal input requirements, we instantiate each world across three monotonic information levels P∈{P0,P1,P2}P\in\{P_{0},P_{1},P_{2}\}:

  1. ❶

    Abstract (P0P_{0}): Primitive geometries and flat shading; retains basic semantics and kinematics to test low-scaffold completion.

  2. ❷

    Simulation (P1P_{1}): Standard physical meshes and basic lighting; serves as the canonical draft-to-video rendering operating point.

  3. ❸

    Previs (P2P_{2}): Dense meshes, full context, and realistic shadows; quantifies headroom while retaining a synthetic-to-real gap.

This axis establishes an information ladder of structural completeness rather than cosmetic image filtering.

Appearance Alignment (AA).

Rich visual cues can either guide rendering or trigger severe source leakage. Therefore, to evaluate adherence to text over deceptive source cues, each granularity PP is paired with three appearance alignment states A∈{AN,AA,AC}A\in\{A_{N},A_{A},A_{C}\}:

  1. ❶

    Neutral (ANA_{N}): Uninformative placeholder shaders (e.g., gray clay), relying solely on text for appearance.

  2. ❷

    Aligned (AAA_{A}): Source appearances match 𝐩i\mathbf{p}_{i} within the precision of the respective granularity level.

  3. ❸

    Conflicting (ACA_{C}): Contradictory source cues (e.g., blue metal vs. target red plastic) to probe source leakage.

Variations affect strictly surface appearance without altering geometry 𝒮i\mathcal{S}_{i}, kinematics 𝒯i\mathcal{T}_{i}, or camera 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i}.

Crossing both axes yields a unified 3×33\times 3 grid of 99 paired inputs 𝒟i(j,k)\mathcal{D}_{i}^{(j,k)} for each world, totaling 48×3×3=43248\times 3\times 3=432 strictly paired test cases. Fixing alignment isolates the marginal gain of draft information (Δ01,Δ12\Delta_{01},\Delta_{12}), while fixing granularity isolates conflict sensitivity and source leakage.

3.4 Evaluation Suite

Standard video metrics (e.g., FVD (Unterthiner et al., 2018)) fail to accurately evaluate both world preservation and visual realization directly. We thus establish an analytical suite across three disentangled dimensions: ➀ world preservation (WP\mathrm{WP}), ➁ rendering fidelity (RF\mathrm{RF}), and ➂ appearance persistence (AP\mathrm{AP}). We report these dimensions separately to preserve diagnostic interpretability, with an additional composite score for overall comparison.

World Preservation (WP\mathrm{WP}).

Grounded in 𝒲i=(𝒮i,𝒯i,ℰi,𝒞i)\mathcal{W}_{i}=(\mathcal{S}_{i},\mathcal{T}_{i},\mathcal{E}_{i},\mathcal{C}_{i}), WP\mathrm{WP} independently benchmarks: ➀ Entity & Layout (𝒮i\mathcal{S}_{i}), using Count Accuracy and trajectory-matched BBox IoU; ➁ Kinematics & Events (𝒯i,ℰi\mathcal{T}_{i},\mathcal{E}_{i}), via Matched Track Coverage, Interaction Success Rate (ISR), and Event Timing Coverage; and ➂ Camera (𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i}), via relative rotation and scale-normalized translation errors against the canonical draft. Metrics evaluate intended topology, ensuring P0P_{0} is not penalized for lacking fine details only introduced in P2P_{2}. Details in Section B.1.

Rendering Fidelity (RF\mathrm{RF}).

Adherence to 𝐩i\mathbf{p}_{i} is evaluated via attribute-level binary QA (Yes/No) across target colors, materials, and lighting, incorporating balanced affirmative/negated probes. Critically, QA judges receive only the target text and generated video, remaining strictly isolated from source drafts to prevent bias. Standard perceptual scores (e.g., Image Quality, Aesthetic) are reported separately as non-gated references VQ\mathrm{VQ}.

Appearance Persistence (AP\mathrm{AP}).

Since maintaining an incorrect appearance over time is not always consistency, we therefore establish a correctness-gated persistence metric:

AP=100|𝒬AP|​∑q∈𝒬APcq⋅sq,\mathrm{AP}=\frac{100}{|\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{AP}}|}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{AP}}}c_{q}\cdot s_{q}, (3)

where cq∈{0,1}c_{q}\in\{0,1\} verifies target attribute realization at an anchor frame, and sq∈{0,1}s_{q}\in\{0,1\} checks whether the identical entity retains that attribute across subsequent timestamps. Credit is awarded if and only if both pass (cq⋅sq=1c_{q}\cdot s_{q}=1).

Grid Diagnostics and Aggregation.

On the full 3×33\times 3 grid, we designate (P1,AN)(P_{1},A_{N}) as the canonical operating point and derive two diagnostic quantities: (i) Conflict Penalty, CP=RF⁡(AA)−RF⁡(AC)\mathrm{CP}=\mathrm{RF}(A_{A})-\mathrm{RF}(A_{C}), measuring performance drop under conflicting cues, and (ii) Source Leakage, SL=Nsource_leaked/Nconflict\mathrm{SL}=N_{\text{source\_leaked}}/N_{\text{conflict}}, quantifying the erroneous persistence of conflicting source attributes.

4 WorldDraft-Primer

The dual correctness criteria of WorldDraft expose an inherent operational dilemma in generative rendering: how to reliably anchor target attributes without corrupting prescribed kinematics. While prompt engineering might seem intuitive, text prompts are inherently spatially agnostic, frequently inducing attribute cross-contamination across multiple entities. Conversely, modifying all draft frames risks destroying the deterministic kinematics and inducing temporal flickering. Leveraging the fact that video diffusion models naturally propagate initial appearances via spatiotemporal attention (Fang et al., 2025; Qi et al., 2026), we propose WorldDraft-Primer, a plug-and-play visual prompting strategy. WorldDraft-Primer intervenes strictly on the initial frame 𝐈1src\mathbf{I}_{1}^{\text{src}}, producing a cued frame 𝐈~1\tilde{\mathbf{I}}_{1}:

𝒟~=(𝐈~1,𝐈2src,…,𝐈Tsrc),𝒱^=𝒢⁡(𝒟~,𝐩),\tilde{\mathcal{D}}=(\tilde{\mathbf{I}}_{1},\mathbf{I}_{2}^{\text{src}},\dots,\mathbf{I}_{T}^{\text{src}}),\qquad\hat{\mathcal{V}}=\mathcal{G}(\tilde{\mathcal{D}},\mathbf{p}), (4)

leaving the remaining T−1T-1 draft frames untouched to preserve the exact physical evolution.

Object Emphasis for World Preservation.

To prevent renderers from dropping small or low-contrast entities, object emphasis introduces sparse, non-intrusive bounding cues. Guided by the prompt 𝐩\mathbf{p}, an open-source VLM (i.e., Qwen3.5 (Yang et al., 2025)) identifies KK critical entities, while an open-vocabulary grounding model predicts their 2D bounding boxes ℬ={𝐛k}k=1K\mathcal{B}=\{\mathbf{b}_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K}. For each box 𝐛k\mathbf{b}_{k}, we generate a binary mask 𝐌kcorner∈{0,1}H×W\mathbf{M}_{k}^{\text{corner}}\in\{0,1\}^{H\times W} outlining minimalist corner brackets strictly around the entity periphery. The structural emphasis signal is formulated as:

Δ​𝐈OE=∑k=1K𝐌kcorner⊙𝐂mono,\Delta\mathbf{I}_{\text{OE}}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{M}_{k}^{\text{corner}}\odot\mathbf{C}_{\text{mono}}, (5)

where 𝐂mono\mathbf{C}_{\text{mono}} is a neutral monochrome tone. Since 𝐌kcorner\mathbf{M}_{k}^{\text{corner}} occupies only narrow peripheral margins without covering entity interiors or physical contact surfaces, it acts purely as a spatial anchor without altering underlying geometry.

Attribute Cueing for Visual Realization.

To steer appearance binding, attribute cueing injects non-textual hints across two levels: (i) entity cues (Δ​𝐈ent\Delta\mathbf{I}_{\text{ent}}), which modulate peripheral brackets with target colors, simplified texture patterns, or coarse specular shading while leaving source interiors visible; and (ii) environment cues (Δ​𝐈env\Delta\mathbf{I}_{\text{env}}), which introduce soft contact shadows, coarse ground textures, or subtle lighting gradients onto supporting surfaces. The composite initial frame 𝐈~1\tilde{\mathbf{I}}_{1} is formulated as:

𝐈~1=𝐈1src⊙(1−𝐌all)+(Δ​𝐈OE+Δ​𝐈ent+Δ​𝐈env)⊙𝐌all,\tilde{\mathbf{I}}_{1}=\mathbf{I}_{1}^{\text{src}}\odot(1-\mathbf{M}_{\text{all}})+\big(\Delta\mathbf{I}_{\text{OE}}+\Delta\mathbf{I}_{\text{ent}}+\Delta\mathbf{I}_{\text{env}}\big)\odot\mathbf{M}_{\text{all}}, (6)

where 𝐌all=∑k𝐌kcorner+𝐌env\mathbf{M}_{\text{all}}=\sum_{k}\mathbf{M}_{k}^{\text{corner}}+\mathbf{M}_{\text{env}} is the aggregate cue mask. Cues remain strictly localized to keep source-target conflicts (ACA_{C}) uncompromised. To avoid generative noise and pixel blurring from diffusion inpainting, all prompts are synthesized programmatically via SVG, ensuring sub-pixel precision and strictly bounded transparency.

5 Experiments

5.1 Experimental Settings

Models.

We benchmark 1212 representative video models on WorldDraft, spanning three primary paradigms across 1010 open-weight architectures: ➀ Generative Renderers: SolarRenderer-33B (Fang et al., 2026), C2R-14B (Gomez-Nogales et al., 2026); ➁ Omni Models: MiniMax-H3-33B (MiniMax, 2025), LynnReal-Omni-32B (Mao et al., 2026), OmniWeaving-8.3B (Pan et al., 2026), VINO-13B (Chen et al., 2026), UniVideo-13B (Wei et al., 2026); and ➂ Controllable Generators: Bernini-R-14B (Team et al., 2026), Wan2.2-VACE-Fun-A14B (Jiang et al., 2025), Wan2.1-VACE-14B (Jiang et al., 2025). We additionally evaluate two leading commercial models: Wan 3.0 (Wan et al., 2025) and Seedance 2.5 (ByteDance Seed, 2025). All models take (𝒟,𝐩)(\mathcal{D},\mathbf{p}) as input, ensuring consistent conditioning.

Evaluations.

Following Section 3.4, we report aggregated dimensional metrics across three core perspectives: ❶ Rendering Performance summarizes overall competence across the full 3×33\times 3 grid via World Preservation (WP\mathrm{WP}: Entity, Motion, Camera), Rendering Fidelity (RF\mathrm{RF}), Visual Quality (VQ\mathrm{VQ}), and Appearance Persistence (AP\mathrm{AP}); ❷ Granularity Gains measures endpoint gains (Δ02\Delta_{02}) across draft levels (P0→P1→P2P_{0}\to P_{1}\to P_{2}) under neutral appearance ANA_{N}; and ❸ Conflict Robustness assesses resilience to conflicting source cues ACA_{C} at P1P_{1} via RFC\mathrm{RF}_{C}, APC\mathrm{AP}_{C}, Conflict Penalty (CP\mathrm{CP}), and Source Leakage (SL\mathrm{SL}). All scores are macro-averaged within each family before aggregating across families on common cohorts. More details in Appendix B.

5.2 Main Results

To systematically characterize the capability boundaries of video generative renderers, we first benchmark 12 video models across the 3×33\times 3 grid of WorldDraft. Key results in Table 1 and Figure 1 yield three primary takeaways:

Takeaway ❶: World preservation and visual realization remain in stark tension.

Models face an inherent dilemma between retaining 4D physics and realizing target appearance. As shown in the Rendering Performance columns of Table 1 and Figure 1, dedicated renderers (e.g., SolarRenderer) lead in Preservation (WP=63.28\text{WP}=63.28) but lag in Realization (RF=69.97\text{RF}=69.97). Conversely, large models (e.g., Wan 3.0) maximize Realization (RF=80.40\text{RF}=80.40) at the cost of severe physical corruption (WP=44.37\text{WP}=44.37, lowest overall). Remarkably, even prevailing commercial leaders like Seedance 2.5, which dominate conventional video benchmarks, fail to top WorldDraft (Overall: 64.7364.73, edged out by 32B LynnReal-Omni at 64.8964.89), compromised by sub-optimal physical preservation (WP=58.66\text{WP}=58.66). This confirms that generic visual scaling does not resolve the dual-correctness challenge.

Takeaway ❷: Richer draft scaffolding anchors structure but impairs appearance binding.

Advancing draft granularity (P0→P2P_{0}\to P_{2} under ANA_{N}) reliably improves structure but yields negative appearance returns. As reported in the Granularity Gains of Table 1 and Figure 1, structural gains (gsg_{s}) are consistently positive across open-weight models (e.g., +18.82+18.82 for Wan2.1-VACE), confirming that dense meshes suppress physical drift. However, appearance (gag_{a}) and binding (gbg_{b}) gains are negative for 9 out of 10 models (e.g., OmniWeaving drops by −14.47/−15.95-14.47\,/\,-15.95), with Seedance 2.5 as the sole exception (+2.51/+3.21+2.51\,/\,+3.21). Denser drafts introduce synthetic shading biases that actively override text-conditioned cross-attention.

Takeaway ❸: Conflicting source cues trigger widespread leakage, exposing fragile disentanglement.

Under contradictory source-target pairs (ACA_{C} at P1P_{1}), models struggle to separate motion scaffolds from surface appearances. As evidenced by the Conflict Robustness metrics in Table 1 and Figure 1, open-weight models suffer large Conflict Penalties (up to 10.6310.63 for OmniWeaving) and rampant color leakage (e.g., 64.17%64.17\% for Wan2.1-VACE and 52.24%52.24\% for UniVideo). Even top commercial and large models (e.g., Wan 3.0, MiniMax-H3) exhibit ∼28%​-​30%\sim 28\%\text{-}30\% leakage, revealing that renderers treat draft pixels as rigid visual constraints rather than overwritable scaffolds.

5.3 Failure Mode Analysis

To diagnose why state-of-the-art models struggle with generative rendering, Figure 4 visualizes representative failure cases from top-performing models ( LynnReal-Omni and Seedance 2.5) on C05 (Occlusion & Reappearance) and A04 (Multi-Entity Orchestration):

Failure Mode ❶: Prompt-driven structural override.

When processing dynamic scenes with complex layouts, models frequently sacrifice draft kinematics to satisfy textual semantics. As illustrated in Figure 4 (a), both LynnReal-Omni and Seedance 2.5 exhibit near-zero Spatial Preservation (consistently scoring ≤18.8\leq 18.8, dipping to 6.26.2). Instead of adhering to the prescribed camera trajectory and warehouse shelving geometry, the models synthesize entirely ungrounded viewpoints and forklift trajectories conditioned solely on the prompt. This demonstrates that models easily devolve from faithful renderers into unconstrained text-to-video generators.

Failure Mode ❷: Deficient spatial reasoning and attribute binding.

Under neutral scaffolds (ANA_{N}), models exhibit weak spatial understanding, failing to parse relative coordinate references and topological arrangements. As shown in Figure 4 (b) , the prompt specifies an ordered 3×43\times 4 color layout across 12 sailboats. Lacking the ability to resolve relative spatial hierarchies (e.g., row depths and left-to-right ordering), the models scramble target colors, causing severe attribute cross-contamination.

Failure Mode ❸: Previs texture latching and conflicting leakage.

Richer drafts and conflicting cues severely disrupt appearance synthesis. In Figure 4 (b), advancing from simulation (P1P_{1}) to previs (P2P_{2}) causes Realization scores to collapse for both models (e.g., LynnReal-Omni drops from 73.173.1 to 46.246.2 under AAA_{A}, and plummets to 17.317.3 under ACA_{C}). Video diffusion models over-attend to the dense synthetic shading and specular highlights of P2P_{2} drafts, treating them as immutable visual priors. Under conflict (ACA_{C}), models either persistently reproduce conflicting source colors (source leakage) or hallucinate unprescribed objects (e.g., LynnReal-Omni synthesizing an extra cluster of green sailboats at P1,ACP_{1},A_{C}) to compensate for text prompts, directly violating draft topology.

5.4 Results with WorldDraft-Primer

Motivated by the failure modes above, we further sought to investigate whether a lightweight test-time strategy can unlock frozen video renderers without retraining. To this end, we evaluate WorldDraft-Primer across representative models ( OmniWeaving and MiniMax-H3) against raw baselines and text prompt engineering (Text PE); results are in Table 2 and Figures 13 and 14.

WorldDraft-Primer consistently enhances both world preservation and visual realization.

As shown in Table 2, WorldDraft-Primer consistently boosts both world preservation and appearance realization across architectures. For OmniWeaving, WorldDraft-Primer enhances Preservation (+2.99+2.99) and Realization (+4.56+4.56) while reducing Source Leakage by 3.42%3.42\%, yielding an Overall gain of +2.51+2.51. For MiniMax-H3, it boosts Realization to 80.2180.21 (+3.83+3.83) and elevates the Overall score to 65.5665.56 (+1.93+1.93), surpassing both LynnReal-Omni (64.8964.89) and the commercial leader Seedance 2.5 (64.7364.73). Conversely, Text PE provides negligible improvements (+0.90+0.90 and +1.26+1.26), limited by the inherent spatial ambiguity of text. Qualitative results in Figures 13 and 14 further confirm these findings: first-frame cues effectively stabilize global camera framing against unprompted zoom-ins, prevent multi-entity attribute cross-contamination (e.g., binding cobalt-blue exclusively to the rightmost ball in B02), and suppress deceptive source color leakage under ACA_{C}.

6 Conclusion

In this work, we explored the emerging division of labor between code-driven simulation and video generation by proposing WorldDraft, a systematic benchmark of 432432 strictly paired test cases across 4848 executable 4D world families. Extensive evaluations across 1212 representative models yield clear answers to our three foundational questions: ➀ world preservation and target appearance realization remain in stark operational tension; ➁ richer draft scaffolding reliably anchors structure but paradoxically impairs appearance fidelity; and ➂ conflicting source cues trigger severe source leakage, exposing fragile cross-modal disentanglement. To mitigate these bottlenecks, we introduce WorldDraft-Primer, a plug-and-play visual prompting strategy that consistently improves both objectives across frozen video renderers. Together, WorldDraft and WorldDraft-Primer establish a foundational stepping stone toward physically grounded generative rendering.

Appendix A More Details of WorldDraft

A.1 Motivation of Each Challenge

Grounded in the dual objectives of world preservation and visual realization, WorldDraft curates dynamic scenarios that jointly impose deterministic physical constraints and multi-modal binding stressors. Evaluating generative renderers on these scenarios probes spatiotemporal reliability across diverse physical regimes: capabilities that conventional static image metrics fundamentally fail to measure. Below, we detail the design motivations behind our six dynamic challenge categories:

Each executable world family in WorldDraft is categorized by its primary physical stressor, while naturally incorporating secondary dynamics. Section A.2 illustrates representative cases and paired draft variants.

A.2 Data Demonstration

Figures 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10 showcase representative cases across all six challenge categories, visualizing the real-world reference footage, target prompt, and the full 3×33\times 3 draft grid (P0→P2×AN,AA,ACP_{0}\to P_{2}\times A_{N},A_{A},A_{C}) for each world.

Appendix B More Details of Evaluation Suite

This section details the formal definitions, score normalization, and aggregation protocols underlying the three evaluation perspectives and the composite score in Table 1. Formally, let c=(P,A)∈Ωc=(P,A)\in\Omega denote an input condition, where Ω={P0,P1,P2}×{AN,AA,AC}\Omega=\{P_{0},P_{1},P_{2}\}\times\{A_{N},A_{A},A_{C}\} represents the full 3×33\times 3 grid of 9 paired configurations across 4848 executable world families {𝒲i}i=148\{\mathcal{W}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{48}. All rate- and accuracy-based metrics are reported on a standard [0,100][0,100] scale.

Shared Temporal & Spatial Protocol.

To ensure fair cross-model comparisons regardless of native frame rates, all evaluations operate on the first 55 seconds of generated videos using absolute timestamp alignment rather than frame indices:

  • •

    Continuous Tracking & Geometry: Dense geometric evaluation (e.g., bounding boxes, tracks, and 6-DoF camera trajectories) is conducted at 88 Hz across 4040 uniformly spaced timestamps (t∈[0,4.875]t\in[0,4.875] s).

  • •

    Sparse Attribute & Event QA: Appearance and interaction probes evaluate 88 key timestamps distributed across the 55-second duration. Following (Huang et al., 2026), question answering is executed via Qwen3.6-27B (Yang et al., 2025). Visual inputs comprise both full frames and reference-grounded entity crops. To eliminate response bias, all probes incorporate strictly balanced affirmative and literal-negation questions.

  • •

    Strict Pre-registration: No output-dependent spatial alignment, post-hoc warping, or scale re-normalization is performed; models are strictly penalized for spatial drift, aspect distortion, or event desynchronization.

Below, we detail the metric composition and normalization for each perspective.

B.1 Rendering Performance

The Rendering Performance section in Table 1 evaluates foundational generation capability across four dimensional scores: Preservation (WP\mathrm{WP}), Realization (RF\mathrm{RF}), Quality (VQ\mathrm{VQ}), and Persistence (AP\mathrm{AP}).

World Preservation.

WP\mathrm{WP} quantifies geometric, physical, and camera fidelity against simulator ground truth, hierarchically combining three sub-components:

WPc=0.40​Ec+0.40​Mc+0.20​Kc.\mathrm{WP}_{c}=0.40E_{c}+0.40M_{c}+0.20K_{c}. (7)

➀ Entity and Layout (EE): We combine Global Count (GC\mathrm{GC}), Local Count (LC\mathrm{LC}), and Bounding Box IoU (BI\mathrm{BI}):

Ec=0.25​GCc+0.25​LCc+0.50​BIc.E_{c}=0.25\,\mathrm{GC}_{c}+0.25\,\mathrm{LC}_{c}+0.50\,\mathrm{BI}_{c}. (8)

GC\mathrm{GC} requires exact instance count agreement across all three sampled timestamps 𝒯cnt={0,2.125,5}​s\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{cnt}}=\{0,2.125,5\}\,\text{s}, while LC\mathrm{LC} evaluates per-frame count accuracy within reference-defined spatial regions:

GC=100𝔼q[∏t∈𝒯cnt𝟏[n^q,t=nq,t]],LC=100𝔼q,t[𝟏[n^q,t=nq,t]].\begin{split}\mathrm{GC}=100\,\mathbb{E}_{q}\left[\prod_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{cnt}}}\mathbf{1}[\hat{n}_{q,t}=n_{q,t}]\right],\\ \mathrm{LC}=100\,\mathbb{E}_{q,t}\left[\mathbf{1}[\hat{n}_{q,t}=n_{q,t}]\right].\end{split} (9)

BI\mathrm{BI} evaluates tracked 2D bounding boxes against simulator-projected amodal 3D entity bounds (including deformation). Entities are detected via SAM3 (Carion et al., 2026) using attribute-agnostic category prompts and matched across time using global Hungarian assignment (IoU threshold ≥0.05\geq 0.05):

BI=100​𝔼e​[1|𝒯e|​∑t∈𝒯eIoU⁡(Be,t,B^a⁡(e),t)].\mathrm{BI}=100\,\mathbb{E}_{e}\left[\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}_{e}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{e}}\mathrm{IoU}(B_{e,t},\hat{B}_{a(e),t})\right]. (10)

Unmatched entities and missing boxes are scored as 00.

➁ Motion and Events (MM): We assess dynamic continuity and physical causality via Matched Track Coverage (TC\mathrm{TC}), Interaction Success Rate (ISR\mathrm{ISR}), and Event Timing Coverage (EC\mathrm{EC}):

Mc=0.25​TCc+0.50​ISRc+0.25​ECc.M_{c}=0.25\,\mathrm{TC}_{c}+0.50\,\mathrm{ISR}_{c}+0.25\,\mathrm{EC}_{c}. (11)

TC=100​𝔼e∈𝒪dyn​[1|𝒯e|​∑t∈𝒯e𝟏​[B^a⁡(e),t​ exists]]\mathrm{TC}=100\,\mathbb{E}_{e\in\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{dyn}}}[\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}_{e}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{e}}\mathbf{1}[\hat{B}_{a(e),t}\text{ exists}]] measures the temporal presence of tracked dynamic entities under the accepted assignment. ISR=100𝔼q[𝟏[a^q=aq] 1[o^q=oq]]\mathrm{ISR}=100\,\mathbb{E}_{q}[\mathbf{1}[\hat{a}_{q}=a_{q}]\,\mathbf{1}[\hat{o}_{q}=o_{q}]] validates that both the dynamic action (aqa_{q}) and its physical outcome (oqo_{q}) are simultaneously correct over 12 uniform frames. EC=100⋅(Nlocalized/Nexpected)\mathrm{EC}=100\cdot(N_{\mathrm{localized}}/N_{\mathrm{expected}}) reports the fraction of causal events whose temporal boundary intervals [tstart,tend][t_{\mathrm{start}},t_{\mathrm{end}}] are successfully localized.

➂ Camera Kinematics (KK): Evaluated across the 8 camera-motion families by estimating 6-DoF trajectories (𝐑⁡(t),𝐭⁡(t))(\mathbf{R}(t),\mathbf{t}(t)) via ViPE (Huang et al., 2025) against the canonical draft. Camera translation is scale-normalized by trajectory peak norm: 𝐮⁡(t)=𝐭⁡(t)/(maxτ⁡‖𝐭⁡(τ)‖2+10−9)\mathbf{u}(t)=\mathbf{t}(t)/(\max_{\tau}\|\mathbf{t}(\tau)\|_{2}+10^{-9}). The camera fidelity score K∈[0,100]K\in[0,100] maps rotation error Rot∈[0,180∘]\mathrm{Rot}\in[0,180^{\circ}] and normalized translation error Trans∈[0,2]\mathrm{Trans}\in[0,2] to:

K=100​[1−12​(Rot180+Trans2)].K=100\left[1-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\mathrm{Rot}}{180}+\frac{\mathrm{Trans}}{2}\right)\right]. (12)

Rendering Fidelity.

Rendering Fidelity evaluates compliance with target color, material, texture, environment, and lighting specifications via balanced binary VLM QA on source-blind judges:

RF=100|𝒬RF|∑q∈𝒬RF𝟏[y^q=yq].\mathrm{RF}=\frac{100}{|\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{RF}}|}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{RF}}}\mathbf{1}[\hat{y}_{q}=y_{q}]. (13)

Each probe evaluates visual evidence at the timestamp where reference entity visibility is maximized.

Visual Quality.

Following VBench (Huang et al., 2024b), we compute frame-level technical and aesthetic quality across all native frames ℱ\mathcal{F} in the first 5 seconds using MUSIQ-SPAQ (Ke et al., 2021) (IQ∈[0,100]\mathrm{IQ}\in[0,100]) and LAION (Schuhmann et al., 2022) aesthetic predictor on CLIP ViT-L/14 (Radford et al., 2021) (AQ=10×Aesthetic∈[0,100]\mathrm{AQ}=10\times\mathrm{Aesthetic}\in[0,100]):

VQ=12​(1|ℱ|​∑f∈ℱIQ⁡(f)+1|ℱ|​∑f∈ℱAQ⁡(f)).\mathrm{VQ}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{|\mathcal{F}|}\sum_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\mathrm{IQ}(f)+\frac{1}{|\mathcal{F}|}\sum_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\mathrm{AQ}(f)\right). (14)

Appearance Persistence.

AP\mathrm{AP} measures whether a correctly instantiated target attribute persistently binds to the entity over time:

AP=100|𝒬AP|​∑q∈𝒬APcq⋅sq,\mathrm{AP}=\frac{100}{|\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{AP}}|}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{AP}}}c_{q}\cdot s_{q}, (15)

where cq∈{0,1}c_{q}\in\{0,1\} verifies attribute realization at a visible anchor frame, and sq∈{0,1}s_{q}\in\{0,1\} verifies temporal consistency across subsequent visible timestamps. An incorrect anchor (cq=0c_{q}=0) strictly zeroes out the score.

Aggregation.

For any metric X∈{WP,RF,VQ,AP}X\in\{\mathrm{WP},\mathrm{RF},\mathrm{VQ},\mathrm{AP}\}, we first macro-average per-video scores across its applicable world family cohort ℐX\mathcal{I}_{X} for each condition c∈𝒞c\in\mathcal{C}:

Xc=1|ℐX|​∑i∈ℐXsi,c(X).X_{c}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{X}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{X}}s^{(X)}_{i,c}. (16)

The four Rendering Performance columns in Table 1 report the mean score over the full 3×33\times 3 grid:

Grid⁡(X)=19​∑c∈𝒞Xc.\operatorname{Grid}(X)=\frac{1}{9}\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}}X_{c}. (17)

Across models, each metric is computed strictly over common valid cohorts for uncompromised fairness.

B.2 Granularity Gains

To quantify how generative renderers benefit from structural scaffolding without confounding appearance cues, we evaluate the geometric information ladder (P0→P1→P2P_{0}\to P_{1}\to P_{2}) strictly under the neutral appearance condition (ANA_{N}). For any metric X∈{WP,RF,AP}X\in\{\mathrm{WP},\mathrm{RF},\mathrm{AP}\}, the paired marginal change between draft granularities PaP_{a} and PbP_{b} is defined as:

Δa​bX=X(Pb,AN)−X(Pa,AN).\Delta_{ab}^{X}=X_{(P_{b},A_{N})}-X_{(P_{a},A_{N})}. (18)

All comparisons enforce strictly paired world families, keeping underlying metric cohorts fixed before constructing WP\mathrm{WP}.

As summarized in Table 1, we report the net endpoint gains from abstract proxy scaffolds (P0P_{0}) to dense preview drafts (P2P_{2}) across three corresponding columns:

gs​(Structure)=Δ02WP,ga​(Appearance)=Δ02RF,gb​(Binding)=Δ02AP.\begin{split}g_{s}\,(\text{Structure})=\Delta_{02}^{\mathrm{WP}},\\ g_{a}\,(\text{Appearance})=\Delta_{02}^{\mathrm{RF}},\\ g_{b}\,(\text{Binding})=\Delta_{02}^{\mathrm{AP}}.\end{split} (19)

Differences preserve their algebraic signs: positive values signify performance gains enabled by richer structural cues, whereas negative values expose degradation or visual interference. While Table 1 focuses on endpoint dynamics Δ02\Delta_{02}, adjacent transitions (Δ01\Delta_{01} and Δ12\Delta_{12}) and per-level absolute scores are documented in supplementary material to diagnose non-monotonicity and saturation behaviors.

B.3 Conflict Robustness

To further evaluate how reliably generative renderers disentangle structural scaffolding from deceptive visual cues, we probe the model’s resistance to contradictory source-target pairs. Fixing the structural scaffold at the canonical simulation operating point (P1P_{1}), Table 1 reports four complementary metrics:

Adherence↑=RF(P1,AC),Retention↑=AP(P1,AC),Penalty​(CP)↓=RF(P1,AA)−RF(P1,AC),Leakage​(SL)↓=SL(P1,AC).\begin{split}\text{Adherence}\uparrow&=\mathrm{RF}_{(P_{1},A_{C})},\\ \text{Retention}\uparrow&=\mathrm{AP}_{(P_{1},A_{C})},\\ \text{Penalty}\;(\mathrm{CP})\downarrow&=\mathrm{RF}_{(P_{1},A_{A})}-\mathrm{RF}_{(P_{1},A_{C})},\\ \text{Leakage}\;(\mathrm{SL})\downarrow&=\mathrm{SL}_{(P_{1},A_{C})}.\end{split} (20)

Adherence and Retention measure absolute target attribute correctness and temporal binding under contradictory conditions (ACA_{C}). Conflict Penalty (CP\mathrm{CP}) quantifies the relative fidelity degradation incurred when source cues transition from aligned (AAA_{A}) to conflicting (ACA_{C}); lower values denote superior immunity to deceptive source distractors.

Source Leakage.

SL\mathrm{SL} explicitly tracks the erroneous persistence of conflicting source colors on target entities. For the set of verified source-color probes 𝒬SL\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{SL}} and their valid timestamps 𝒯q\mathcal{T}_{q}, it is formulated as:

SL=100|𝒬SL|∑q∈𝒬SL1|𝒯q|∑t∈𝒯q𝟏[y^q,t=Yes],\mathrm{SL}=\frac{100}{|\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{SL}}|}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{SL}}}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}_{q}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{q}}\mathbf{1}[\hat{y}_{q,t}=\text{Yes}], (21)

where y^q,t=Yes\hat{y}_{q,t}=\text{Yes} indicates the active presence of the contradictory source color. Probes are constructed from audited source materials across 4848 world families with explicit color contradictions. Note that low SL\mathrm{SL} does not trivially imply correct target realization.

B.4 Composite Overall Metric

To provide a unified ranking across diverse model paradigms, the Overall column in Table 1 integrates the three diagnostic perspectives via pre-registered weights:

Overall=0.50​R+0.25​G+0.25​Crob,\mathrm{Overall}=0.50\,R+0.25\,G+0.25\,C_{\mathrm{rob}}, (22)

allocating 50%50\% to foundational rendering capability, 25%25\% to structural granularity responsiveness, and 25%25\% to source-target conflict disentanglement. All underlying metrics are bounded in [0,100][0,100]:

Rendering Score (RR).

Within each condition c∈𝒞c\in\mathcal{C}, we combine the macro-averaged dimensional scores using a weighted geometric mean before averaging across the 3×33\times 3 grid R=19​∑c∈𝒞ScR=\frac{1}{9}\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}}S_{c}:

Sc=100⋅(WPc100)0.40​(RFc100)0.20​(APc100)0.30​(VQc100)0.10.\begin{split}S_{c}=100\cdot(\frac{\mathrm{WP}_{c}}{100})^{0.40}(\frac{\mathrm{RF}_{c}}{100})^{0.20}(\frac{\mathrm{AP}_{c}}{100})^{0.30}(\frac{\mathrm{VQ}_{c}}{100})^{0.10}.\end{split} (23)

The geometric mean strictly penalizes degenerate shortcuts (e.g., preserving kinematics by completely ignoring target prompts, or satisfying prompts by severely corrupting the 4D world), rewarding renderers that achieve balanced dual-correctness.

Granularity Score (GG).

Since individual endpoint gains g∈{gs,ga,gb}g\in\{g_{s},g_{a},g_{b}\} lie in [−100,100][-100,100], we linearly normalize them to a standard [0,100][0,100] scale (where 5050 denotes zero net change) before computing their unweighted average:

G=13​∑g∈{gs,ga,gb}(50+g2)=50+gs+ga+gb6.G=\frac{1}{3}\sum_{g\in\{g_{s},g_{a},g_{b}\}}\left(50+\frac{g}{2}\right)=50+\frac{g_{s}+g_{a}+g_{b}}{6}. (24)

Conflict Robustness Score (CrobC_{\mathrm{rob}}).

We unify the four conflict metrics into a higher-is-better index in [0,100][0,100]:

Crob=14[RF(P1,AC)+AP(P1,AC)+(100−max(CP,0))+(100−SL(P1,AC))].\begin{split}C_{\mathrm{rob}}=\frac{1}{4}[\mathrm{RF}_{(P_{1},A_{C})}+\mathrm{AP}_{(P_{1},A_{C})}+\\ \big(100-\max(\mathrm{CP},0)\big)+\big(100-\mathrm{SL}_{(P_{1},A_{C})}\big)].\end{split} (25)

Here, the Conflict Penalty CP\mathrm{CP} is clipped at zero to avoid rewarding negative penalties (which arise from statistical variance rather than genuine robustness), while source leakage SL\mathrm{SL} is inverted.

While the Overall score offers a holistic summary, the underlying gains and penalties are inherently dependent on each model’s baseline operating performance. Therefore, the standalone columns in Table 1 remain essential for diagnosing individual failure modes and capability trade-offs.

B.5 Analysis of Metric-Human Alignment

To validate the VLM evaluation protocol part of WorldDraft, we compare algorithmic decisions against blind annotations from five independent human judges on randomly sampled test cases, using majority voting as ground truth. As shown in Figure 11, automated metrics achieve strong human agreement across all six dimensions, ranging from 87.5%87.5\% to 94.2%94.2\% (averaging 91.0%91.0\%). Appearance probes exhibit the highest concordance (RF:94.2%\mathrm{RF}:94.2\%, SL:92.5%\mathrm{SL}:92.5\%, AP:91.5%\mathrm{AP}:91.5\%), while physical and count metrics remain highly reliable (ISR:90.8%\mathrm{ISR}:90.8\%, GC:89.2%\mathrm{GC}:89.2\%, LC:87.5%\mathrm{LC}:87.5\%). This validates our automated benchmark suite as a faithful surrogate for human judgment.

Appendix C More Details of WorldDraft-Primer

C.1 Case Demonstration and Analysis

Figures 13 and 14 visualize qualitative rollouts across the 3×33\times 3 grid for B02 (Newton’s Cradle) and D02 (Water-Tank Tower). Across both scenarios, WorldDraft-Primer visibly improves adherence to input drafts: it stabilizes global camera framing against erratic zoom-ins, suppresses ball dropouts in B02 while precisely isolating target colors to the rightmost sphere, and preserves surrounding town layouts in D02 while mitigating deceptive ACA_{C} roof colors.

Capacity Dependency and Method Positioning.

Crucially, WorldDraft-Primer operates as a lightweight visual prompting strategy whose efficacy remains inherently tethered to the underlying base model. On weaker architectures (e.g., OmniWeaving), the model occasionally struggles to assimilate the injected first-frame cues into photorealistic textures, sometimes faintly echoing prompt brackets across subsequent frames. Furthermore, under dense previs drafts (P2P_{2}), strong synthetic priors can still bias the renderer toward artificial, plastic-like shading. Ultimately, WorldDraft-Primer serves as an analytical proof-of-concept demonstrating that test-time visual cues can steer frozen video models. Fully overcoming dense prior interference and enabling seamless prompt assimilation remain important challenges for future work.

C.2 Ablation Study of WorldDraft-Primer

To dissect the individual contributions of Object Emphasis (Δ​IOE\Delta I_{\mathrm{OE}}) and Attribute Cueing (Δ​Ient+Δ​Ienv\Delta I_{\mathrm{ent}}+\Delta I_{\mathrm{env}}), we ablate each component on MiniMax-H3 across the full benchmark. As shown in Figure 12, the two mechanisms exhibit remarkable orthogonality and synergy:

Removing corner brackets (w/o Object Emphasis) causes a sharp collapse across all spatial metrics: Global Count drops from 30.0230.02 to 28.7028.70, Local Count from 45.4245.42 to 43.4343.43, and BBox IoU from 16.7016.70 to 15.9715.97 (falling back near the base model), demonstrating that geometric brackets are indispensable for anchoring coordinates and preventing entity dropouts. Conversely, removing color and environmental hints (w/o Attribute Cueing) cripples appearance metrics, dropping RF from 80.2180.21 to 76.6176.61 and AP from 73.8473.84 to 70.5370.53, while increasing Source Leakage to 26.75%26.75\%. Crucially, integrating both components achieves the highest score across all six metrics simultaneously, confirming that our design decouples spatial trajectory anchoring from surface attribute binding without mutual interference.

C.3 Text Prompt Engineering Baseline (Text PE)

Our Text PE baseline adapts Video Prompt Optimization (VPO) (Cheng et al., 2025) for generative rendering under four strict controls: (i) the target prompt is optimized once per world family (pi→pi′p_{i}\to p^{\prime}_{i}) and shared across all nine factorial conditions to preserve paired design; (ii) the meta-prompt enriches descriptive appearance attributes while explicitly delegating kinematics, spatial layout, and camera motion to the draft; (iii) generations use identical random seeds, drafts, and model inference templates; and (iv) all evaluations strictly assess adherence to the original prompt pip_{i}, preventing spurious metric shifts.

C.4 System Prompt for Visual Prompting

To automate first-frame cue generation of WorldDraft-Primer, we deploy Qwen3.5-27B (Yang et al., 2025) as an agentic visual grounding reasoner. Given the target prompt and sampled draft frames, the agent is instructed to: (i) identify and ground key entity boxes in the first frame based on geometry and motion rather than conflicting source colors; (ii) extract target attributes (e.g., specified colors and patterns) from the prompt; and (iii) programmatically invoke cropping and SVG drawing tools to generate minimalist corner brackets and localized attribute cues. Appendix D Exhibition Board

To provide an exhaustive qualitative autopsy across physical regimes while adhering to submission file size limits, complete high-resolution 3×33\times 3 grid rollouts across all six dynamic challenge categories are hosted on our interactive project page: https://haroldchen19.github.io/WorldDraft-site. Below, we analyze representative failure cases from the top-four benchmarked models ( LynnReal-Omni, Seedance 2.5, MiniMax-H3, and Wan 3.0). Even among these top performers, models systematically struggle to simultaneously satisfy visual plausibility, 4D structural preservation, and target attribute realization. These qualitative results substantiate three primary insights:

Appearance realism decouples from structural fidelity.

Superficial visual quality frequently masks severe structural violations. In C05 (Occlusion & Reappearance), models synthesize photorealistic warehouse textures and forklifts, yet arbitrarily rearrange shelving aisles, alter obstacle depths, and distort occlusion orders. Similarly, in A01 (Multi-Entity Orchestration), MiniMax-H3 introduces unprompted camera rotations away from the canonical top-down view, while Wan 3.0 in F03 transforms dense, orderly domino arrays into sparse irregular blocks. These cases confirm that achieving high visual quality or satisfying isolated appearance QA queries does not equate to faithful generative rendering.

Granularity returns are multidimensionally asymmetric.

Increasing draft granularity does not guarantee monotonic improvements across all generative axes. While detailed geometry (P2P_{2}) helps resolve local entity contours, it frequently induces composition drift, under-stylization, or degraded appearance binding. In E03 (Multi-Stage Dynamics), MiniMax-H3 under ANA_{N} zooms in excessively as granularity increases from P0P_{0} to P2P_{2}, causing the umbrella to drift out of frame. In B05 (Multi-Stage Dynamics), Seedance 2.5 fails to photorealistically stylize dense drafts at P1P_{1} and P2P_{2}, retaining synthetic, toy-like block artifacts despite explicit prompts for painted steel. Higher input granularity thus alters the model’s visual attention, often trading global framing stability for local geometric detail.

Source leakage persists across dense scaffolds.

Resolving contradictory appearance cues (ACA_{C}) requires renderers to simultaneously overwrite misleading pixels while retaining underlying kinematics. However, models consistently treat source colors as uneditable geometry: in C05 at (P1,AC)(P_{1},A_{C}), MiniMax-H3 replicates the deceptive red bodywork of the draft rather than synthesizing the target yellow; in E03 at (P2,AC)(P_{2},A_{C}), Seedance 2.5 faithfully tracks the complex umbrella canopy but tenaciously retains its conflicting red-and-white stripes, failing to bind target yellow and navy-blue hues. Crucially, even when the draft provides dense, unambiguous geometric scaffolds (P2P_{2}), models remain vulnerable to source color leakage, underscoring the urgent need for explicit cross-modal disentanglement mechanisms.
